Council Briefing

Assembled from the ATNI Energy Task Forces site.

Nothing chosen yet. Tick plates and checklists at left; the packet builds here.

Measured
977 figures read from a source and cited by claim id; 678 of them partly verified, each with its limit printed.
Modeled
The comparison model, formula rows. Figures marked modeled are computed from the receipts and the reader's settings, not measured.
Chosen by the reader
Every plate at its defaults.

Contents

  1. An hour of chat and an hour of video overlap: about 15 and 14 Wh, 12 Wh of each your own screen and router
  2. A text prompt is seconds to minutes of streaming; an agent session is hours on every yardstick
  3. An average weekly ChatGPT user's text prompts cost about 1 Wh a day in the data center, an illustration
  4. All of ChatGPT's text messages are a few tenths of a terawatt-hour a year; the buildout adds hundreds
  5. By 2035, BLS projects +34.6 percent for data scientists and -25.5 for data entry keyers
  6. By 2035, BLS projects +25.1 percent in computing and hosting and -4 in office and administrative support
  7. Studies disagree, and every row measures a different thing
  8. In nine months, capital spending passed operating cash flow at Amazon: 176 billion dollars against 114
  9. Amazon spent 132 billion dollars against 123 billion of cash and securities; Apple spent 9 against 137
  10. Google's electricity rose 37 percent in 2025 to 43.6 TWh
  11. For 2026, Amazon guides to about 220 billion dollars and Alphabet to 195 to 205; Apple and NVIDIA give none
  12. Market capitalization on 10/30/2026 ran from about 1,572 billion dollars (Meta) to 5,008 (Apple)
  13. The Council puts data centers and chip fabs at 2,475 aMW in 2030, in a region using 22,000 today
  14. EIA's baseline puts data center servers at 105 billion kWh in 2025 and 178 by 2030
  15. LBNL counts 192 TWh for US data centers in 2024 and 649 by 2030 in its reference case
  16. The IEA counts 485 TWh for the world's data centers in 2025 and about 945 by 2030 in its base case
  17. 15 editions of 18 put 2023 US electricity sales high; 7 editions of 9 put commercial sales low
  18. Power, water, and carbon have agency figures; land, heat, and materials have one or two modeled ones
  19. A 100 MW site's evaporative cooling consumes about 190 to 810 million liters a year on site
  20. On a consumption basis, operators report 0.27 to 1.15 liters per kWh
  21. The filings read put 6 of 83 named proposals on BLM public land
  22. Walla Walla County's May to September daytime high averages about 87 F in 2040 to 2059, up from 84 F
  23. A 100 MW site implies about 70 to 200 construction workers at peak and 15 to 35 permanent staff
  24. 125 MW at 0.8 load factor is about 0.88 TWh a year, 0.45 percent of the region
  25. Efficiency, solar, and electrification lead 44 Tribes' public plans; no finding concerns offshore wind or marine energy
  26. 4 dated deadlines through 08/31/2028, the first on 11/05/2026; 8 more programs carry no date in the catalog

Sources for: A 100 MW site implies about 70 to 200 construction workers at peak and 15 to 35 permanent staff

  1. jb-023Megawatts, but few permanent jobs? An agent-assisted evidence review of the data-centre construction cliff, Smart and Sustainable Built Environment (Emerald), published 09/02/2026. partly verified: A modeled range for direct on-site workers from a synthesis of studies that the paper compares within, and does not pool across, evidence families; developer-announced figures run higher, at 1.3 to 3.6 per megawatt.
  2. jb-024Megawatts, but few permanent jobs? An agent-assisted evidence review of the data-centre construction cliff, Smart and Sustainable Built Environment (Emerald), published 09/02/2026. partly verified: Direct permanent staff only, from the same synthesis; the range matches another benchmark, so the two are not independent.
  3. jb-035We studied 1,584 data centers and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth, The Conversation, published 10/27/2026. partly verified: A county-level estimate that counts all local nonconstruction jobs, not data center staff, and shows association rather than cause; it is about ten times the on-site staffing ratio.
  4. jb-028Potential Economic Impact of a Hyperscale Data Center in Montana, University of Montana Bureau of Business and Economic Research, published 10/29/2026. partly verified: Modeled for a hypothetical Montana campus in a study commissioned for a proposed project, not measured; operating jobs do not scale in proportion to size.
  5. jb-029Potential Economic Impact of a Hyperscale Data Center in Montana, University of Montana Bureau of Business and Economic Research, published 10/29/2026. partly verified: Modeled for a hypothetical Montana campus in a study commissioned for a proposed project, not measured; twice the megawatts gives about 1.5 times the direct jobs.
  6. jb-081Understanding Oregon's Data Center Industry: An Evidence Based Assessment (full report), ECOnorthwest (prepared for the Lemelson Foundation; draft presented to the Oregon Department of Energy 07/31/2026), published 10/05/2026. partly verified: A consultant's estimate built on state employment data, not an agency count; it covers direct operations workers only and excludes contractors, construction workers, and corporate staff.
  7. jb-082Understanding Oregon's Data Center Industry: An Evidence Based Assessment (full report), ECOnorthwest (prepared for the Lemelson Foundation; draft presented to the Oregon Department of Energy 07/31/2026), published 10/05/2026. partly verified: A consultant's estimate built on state employment data, not an agency count; it is the Eastern Oregon share of the statewide direct operations total.
  8. jb-085Understanding Oregon's Data Center Industry: An Evidence Based Assessment (full report), ECOnorthwest (prepared for the Lemelson Foundation; draft presented to the Oregon Department of Energy 07/31/2026), published 10/05/2026. partly verified: Modeled from construction spending, not counted; the jobs are temporary, and the same report puts the direct input at about 1,913 workers once projects are annualized over 18 to 36 months.
  9. jb-084Understanding Oregon's Data Center Industry: An Evidence Based Assessment (full report), ECOnorthwest (prepared for the Lemelson Foundation; draft presented to the Oregon Department of Energy 07/31/2026), published 10/05/2026. partly verified: Modeled with IMPLAN multipliers, not counted; the result depends on the model's assumptions and is not an agency count.
  10. jb-0732026 tax preference review: Data Centers in Urban Counties (preliminary report, July 2026), Washington Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee (JLARC), published 06/25/2026. partly verified: Self-reported by tax-exemption beneficiaries and not verified by the Department of Revenue; the total is cumulative for 2023 and 2024, and the auditors say it is unclear whether the jobs meet the program's requirements.
  11. jb-0742026 tax preference review: Data Centers in Urban Counties (preliminary report, July 2026), Washington Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee (JLARC), published 06/25/2026. partly verified: Self-reported counts of jobs, not full-time equivalents; project length, wages, and labor hours are not reported.

  13. jb-0802026 tax preference review: Data Centers in Urban Counties (preliminary report, July 2026), Washington Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee (JLARC), published 06/25/2026. partly verified: Arithmetic on this page: total beneficiary savings divided by self-reported permanent jobs; it ignores the temporary jobs and the local tax base gain, and the legislative auditors do not state it.

Consent

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. Have citizens been asked, in a survey, town hall, or referendum, and what did they say? Cherokee Nation’s task force collected 1,593 survey responses from citizens before the Principal Chief acted.
  2. Who is the true counterparty and end user: developer, hyperscale operator, or investor? Has the Council seen every non-disclosure agreement, and does any NDA keep officials from speaking with their own people?
  3. Does the proposal reach ceded lands, Treaty-protected places, or cultural sites, and have Treaty and cultural resource staff reviewed it before any inquiry is answered?
  4. Is “no” or “not yet” still an available answer at every stage?
  1. pdc-026Report on the Impact of Data Centers on the Economy and Natural Environment of the Cherokee Nation Reservation, Cherokee Nation, Principal Chief's Task Force on Data Centers, published 06/30/2026. partly verified: The report counts survey responses collected through the Nation's Gadugi portal and does not say how respondents were chosen, so the result is not shown to represent all citizens.

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Settings chosen by the reader, sources checked 11/04/2026.

Land

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. What is the land status (trust, allotment, fee), and does the Tribe have approved HEARTH Act leasing regulations? For counsel: does the existing leasing code cover a data center and its generation, or is an amendment, a Tribal Energy Resource Agreement, or a Section 17 entity the better vehicle (BIA, HEARTH Act)?
  2. What lease term is requested, and what happens to the land and improvements when it ends?
  3. Which law governs the facility, Tribal environmental, zoning, and permitting codes or state and local ones, and who enforces it?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Settings chosen by the reader, sources checked 11/04/2026.

Water

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. What is the cooling design, and how much water does it withdraw and consume across all operating phases? Is closed-loop or air cooling a binding term, not a promise? Try the cooling instrument.
  2. What is the source (surface, aquifer, or municipal), and what is its hydrological connection to salmon-bearing streams?
  3. Under drought and low-flow conditions, could withdrawals push streams below what fish passage, spawning, or rearing need? Has cumulative withdrawal with existing agricultural, municipal, and industrial users been assessed?
  4. Have Tribal water rights and instream flow needs been specifically accounted for? For counsel: where a reserved or Treaty water right is unquantified, what must be filed, and where, to keep a new large user from being permitted ahead of it (DOJ, Federal Reserved Water Rights)?
  5. What is discharged, at what temperature, with what chemicals, into what receiving water, and are there Tribal fishing sites or cold-water refuges downstream?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Settings chosen by the reader, sources checked 11/04/2026.

Power

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. How many megawatts at full load, and who generates it? Is on-site generation fossil-fueled, and what are the air permit and emissions commitments, including backup generators?
  2. Will the load add pressure on the hydropower system during peak or emergency conditions, when fish protections are suspended?
  3. Who pays for transmission, substation, and fiber upgrades, and who owns them afterward?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Rates

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. Is there a large-load tariff that assigns the facility’s full cost of service, with minimum billing, collateral, and exit charges? Oregon’s POWER Act, Grant PUD’s terms, and NorthWestern’s filing are reference points (Oregon PUC; Grant PUD; NorthWestern Energy).
  2. Will Tribal members’ electricity bills rise, and has a Tribal utility or the serving utility modeled it before signing?

Jobs

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. What are the realistic permanent jobs and wages? The Department of Energy puts permanent staffing at “a few to a few dozen” per facility (DOE FAQ). Try the jobs instrument.
  2. Are local hiring, apprenticeship, and training commitments written into the agreement, with a public dashboard and audit rights?

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy).   1. If Tribal data will be hosted, under what terms? Which TSDF tier does each dataset carry, and does the contract bar the operator from using, training on, or retaining it (Resolution #2026-034, PDF)?
  2. Whose law governs the data, and in whose courts?

Exit Terms

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. What happens if demand for AI computing contracts: minimum payments regardless of occupancy, parent guarantees, decommissioning bonds, and reversion of improvements?
  2. For counsel: what is the narrowest waiver of sovereign immunity a Tribe or Tribal entity can grant (forum, remedies, assets reachable, term), and could an arbitration or governing-law clause operate as a broader waiver than intended?
  3. Has independent legal, financial, and technical counsel, not paid by the developer, reviewed the full deal?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.
